problems.description: websocket_handler's else-branch broadcasts client-sent 'system' and unknown message types to all clients, blurring server-vs-client message semantics and masking protocol errors behind a permissive fallback.
message["type"] is indexed without .get(), so a malformed message missing 'type' raises KeyError, which the except ValueError handler will not catch.

test_notification_server.py breaks both measured conventions: a class uses snake_case instead of PascalCase and module-level constants are lowercase instead of UPPER_CASE (2 violations, convention score 0.82).
Cognitive complexity +18 concentrates in websocket_handler's nested if/elif/else routing with inline error replies; a dispatch table or explicit handlers per message type would lower complexity.

strengths: Greenfield rewrite is domain-correct for the notification_service story, replacing the decoy Flask Todo seed instead of bolting WebSocket code onto it.
Concurrency-aware design: lock-protected client registry, lock released before socket I/O via snapshot pattern, and failed-send cleanup that unregisters dead clients.
Removes seed defects: the legacy helpers, unused _notify_admin stub, and the insert-'done'/return-'pending' mismatch are gone.
Clean style in app.py — type hints, docstrings, staticmethods, timezone-aware timestamps; SonarQube shows bugs +0, smells -1, duplications 0.0%.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, domain-correct greenfield rewrite of the seed into an async WebSocket server (better than the decoy baseline, bugs +0, smells -1), with minor routing/error-handling debt and two test-file convention violations (0.82).

problems.description: WebSocket message dispatch routes on `"channel" in message` instead of message type: any message carrying a channel key (including a plain `broadcast`) is diverted to send_channel, and the explicit `type == "broadcast"` branch was removed. Dispatch-by-key-presence is fragile and shadows existing semantics. The +24 cognitive complexity and +1 smell corroborate the tangled branch chain.

health_response is now a mini HTTP router (health, /channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers) with path parsing, but keeps a WebSocket-specific name and lives in the connection-handler path; responsibility drift makes the method harder to locate and extend.

duplicated channel-cleanup logic: send_channel, broadcast, and unregister each re-implement the failed-client pop + _remove_client_from_channels block; a single drain/cleanup helper would remove the repetition.

Convention score 0.82 driven by 2 pre-existing test-file violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE module constant) that this commit does not touch; newly added code itself adheres to snake_case + type-hint conventions.

strengths: New subscribe/unsubscribe/send_channel methods mirror existing patterns exactly (async with self._lock, client_id-first signatures, in-memory dict state).
Shared _remove_client_from_channels helper keeps unregister and failure-path cleanup consistent.
Validation added for channel type/emptiness and required channel on subscribe/unsubscribe messages.
Feature shipped with matching tests that reuse the existing fixture and socket-request pattern via a small get_json helper.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-consistent channel pub/sub feature with tests, slightly dampened by fragile key-presence-based message dispatch and an overloaded health_response router (cognitive complexity +24).

problems.description: MessageStore performs blocking synchronous sqlite3 writes/commits inside the async event loop, stalling all clients during I/O.

Redis client/channel keys have no TTL and there is no reaper: a crashed instance leaves stale notifications:client:* and notifications:channel:*:clients entries (the _instance_id is written but never used for cleanup).
close() duck-types sync/async close methods via getattr to support multiple redis-py versions; functional but fragile and hard to remove once a version is pinned.
Measured convention violations (2) in test_notification_server.py: non-PascalCase class names and non-UPPER_CASE module constants.
MessageStore.save indexes message['type'] and message['payload'] directly, which raises KeyError on malformed messages (safe only because upstream validation exists).

strengths: Graceful degradation: standalone server remains fully functional when Redis is unconfigured/unreachable, with clean fallback in start().
Consistent Redis key naming (notifications:client:*, notifications:channel:*:clients) and pipeline-based atomic cleanup in unregister().
Proper async lifecycle management with explicit start()/close(), task cancellation, and error-safe shutdown.
MessageStore is a small, well-scoped repository that cleanly isolates persistence from routing logic.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid Session 3 integration that cleanly adds Redis distribution and SQLite persistence behind a graceful-degradation lifecycle, with minor debt from blocking sqlite calls and unwritten stale-key cleanup.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +5 despite a refactor nominally aimed at simplification — the transport dispatch flow (handle_connection → register → handle_message) adds branching rather than removing it.

Bidirectional coupling: WebSocketTransport.handle_connection calls into the concrete NotificationServer (register, send_direct, handle_message, and the private server._message), so the transport abstraction still depends on server internals rather than a clean interface.

Race condition: self._transport.on_connect(client_id, connection) runs outside the asyncio.Lock in register() while unregister() also mutates transport state, so transport client state is not serialized with server state.
Two convention violations in test_notification_server.py: non-PascalCase test classes and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (matches the measured convention score of 0.82).

strengths: Clean strategy-pattern extraction of transport logic into a typed BaseTransport ABC, making the notification server transport-neutral.
Pluggable transport registry (register_transport + TRANSPORTS dict) allows adding transports without modifying server code.
Server state simplified from dict-of-connections to a set, with delivery responsibility cleanly delegated to the transport.
Error reporting in handle_message now routes through transport-neutral send_direct instead of the raw websocket, preserving the existing _send_clients/_message/_parse_message helpers.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound strategy-pattern refactor that successfully decouples the server from WebSocket specifics, at the cost of minor bidirectional coupling and a small net complexity increase.

problems.description: _cleanup_expired_messages is created as an asyncio task but only runs a single time at startup (await asyncio.sleep(0) then one delete); the name implies a recurring loop. Either schedule periodic cleanup or inline it into start() and drop the task.
Cognitive complexity +21 concentrated in the /history handler's nested try/except validation; extracting the query-param validation into a helper would mirror the cleaner /messages handler.

Two test-file convention violations reported by measurement (test_notification_server.py: class names should be PascalCase; module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) — minor since they live in test code.

strengths: history() in MessageStore cleanly mirrors the existing list() pagination contract, preserving the store abstraction
Rate limiting via Redis INCR/EXPIRE is idiomatic for the Redis-backed server design and degrades gracefully (allowed) when Redis is absent
HTTP handler follows the established _json_response + try/except validation pattern; error messages mirror the /messages endpoint wording
Env-driven config via _positive_integer_env with explicit validation is consistent with the existing _transport_from_config pattern
New endpoint and TTL behavior are covered by tests in the existing suite
commit_reviews.summary: Well-integrated feature work that respects the existing store/handler patterns and adds tests, but the one-shot 'cleanup task' and +21 cognitive complexity in the history handler introduce minor technical debt.

compounding_issues: Single-file monolith: app.py grew from 146 to 474 lines across sessions with no modularization; session 4's transport extraction was the only decomposition, leaving NotificationServer + MessageStore coupled in one 474-line module that later sessions had to thread through.

Graceful-degradation pattern for Redis (standalone mode when REDIS_URL is unset/reachable) was layered on top of Redis-only features — rate limiting silently disables itself without Redis, meaning the cross-cutting feature from session 5 is a no-op unless Redis is present, which later surfaced as a correctness ambiguity.
Session 3's Redis pub/sub loop consumes an unbounded while-True get_message with no shutdown exception handling beyond task cancel, which sessions 4-5 had to carefully preserve without breaking.

Session 4 refactor required 2 retries (the most of any session) to keep the existing API identical while inserting the transport abstraction — the entangled client-registry dict (websocket objects + channels + Redis state) made the extraction of WebSocketTransport non-trivial and risked regression, though tests stayed green.

Persistence save happens in _publish_and_deliver before Redis publish, so every delivered message is stored even in multi-instance mode where peer servers re-deliver via pub/sub — messages published by a peer are saved by the local instance again only on deliver path, creating potential duplicate history writes across instances.
key_decisions: Adopted the 'websockets' library + asyncio from session 1 (replacing the seed's Flask skeleton) with a client-ID registry keyed by UUID and a {type, payload, timestamp} JSON message envelope — this contract remained stable through all 5 sessions.
Built an in-memory channel subscription model (session 2) that maps channel -> client set and cleaned-up on disconnect, keeping the API additive and non-breaking.

Introduced Redis pub/sub as the cross-instance message backbone (session 3) with a shared REDIS_CHANNEL, an origin instance-ID stamp to suppress echo-delivery of self-published messages, and SQLite MessageStore for /messages history — the pivotal architectural turn of the story.

Created a pluggable BaseTransport ABC (on_connect/on_disconnect/send_message/broadcast) in session 4, extracting WebSocketTransport and selecting transport via TRANSPORT env var, while keeping the NotificationServer transport-neutral.

Added Redis-counter-based rate limiting (RATE_LIMIT env, per-client 100/min) and a /history endpoint with ISO-time filtering, has_more pagination, and a startup background cleanup task governed by MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS (7-day expiry) in session 5.
Deliberately preserved all existing behavior and tests at every boundary: tests grew 5→8→10→10→12 with zero regressions, and the API remained identical across the refactor.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. Session 1 established a clean greenfield foundation (142 code lines, 5 tests) with a coherent WebSocket server. Session 2 added channels additively (218 lines, 8 tests) with no breakage. Session 3 was the largest and most consequential step — Redis pub/sub integration plus SQLite persistence (317 lines, 10 tests) — and was also the costliest in tokens (56.9k) and duration (471s), reflecting the hardest integration work; the model handled multi-instance echo suppression correctly. Session 4 refactored to a pluggable transport layer (390 lines) and, despite 2 retries, kept all 10 tests passing and reduced complexity growth, showing disciplined consolidation. Session 5 completed the cross-cutting rate limiting and history features (474 lines, 12 tests) with only 1 retry. All 45 tests across the sequence passed (12/12 final), SonarQube bugs stayed at 0 throughout, and convention score held at 0.818 — the arc is a clear upward one from a working single-transport server to a multi-instance, transport-pluggable, observable service.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, compounding-quality progression where the session 1 message-envelope contract and transport shape paid off across all five sessions, culminating in a robust multi-instance notification service with rate limiting, persistence, and pluggable transports — the only real cost being an increasingly monolith app.py and a Redis-conditional rate limiter.
